sections.html:
• Name: Chopstick snail
  • Other names: Long Nose
  • Scientific name: Stenomelania torulosa (synonyms Melanoides torulosus, Thiara torulosa)
  • Optimal tank size: 40 litres
  • Breeding: Very difficult
  • Nitrate: less than 40 ppm
  • Diet: algae eater/detritivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Colour: from light olive to dark brown

Chopstick snails are very hardy and easy to care for, so they can be recommended even for beginners. They do not breed in freshwater, which makes them an excellent choice with a controlled population.

The ecology of Stenomelania torulosa is poorly researched and much is still unknown about these snails. Even though they are fairly common in South Asia, they are still rather rare on the Western pet trade market.
Stenomelania torulosa can be found in India, Ceylon, the Andaman Islands, the Malay Archipelago, Taiwan, the Philippines, the Solomon Islands and Tamil Nadu: Porto Novo.

Their habitat is areas near rivers and streams.

The maximum population density of this species has been recorded beyond the mangrove in a freshwater environment where saltwater penetrates only occasionally during extremely high tides.

The minimum recommended tank size is 40 litres. They are big and quite active, and need a lot of room to crawl, eat and explore.

Anything smaller and you may have feeding problems, as there will not be enough algae and biofilm in the tank. In addition, keeping stable water parameters in smaller tanks can be a challenge even for experienced aquarists.

Care is quite easy and straightforward. They are low-maintenance and can withstand varied water parameters. Cycle the tank before bringing snails home, then check water quality with a test kit.

Acclimate them carefully, as with all invertebrates, very slowly; 2–3 hours is generally good enough.

Be careful with chemicals such as copper. Snails do not tolerate copper-based products because of the reaction between the snail's mucus and the copper.

Temperature: they can live in a wide range of 20–30°C, but the optimal range is 24–27°C.

pH: aim for 7.0–8.0. Most snails do not like staying in acidic water (below 7.0) for weeks; acidic water slowly dissolves the shell and makes it fragile.

Hardness: 1–12 GH. The harder the water, the better for their shells.

Salinity: Stenomelania sp. is mainly active in freshwater and more or less rests when salinity rises. They usually retract into the shell in seawater and regain activity immediately when moved to freshwater.

Nitrate: less than 40 ppm.

Filtration: no special requirements; a filter suited to the size of the tank is fine. In small tanks, sponge or matten filters are recommended: they are cheap, easy to maintain and provide a lot of surface to graze on.

Lighting: they are nocturnal, so lighting is mostly a matter of taste. If you keep plants, adapt the light to the plants' needs (and/or algae if wanted).

Substrate: ideally one that lets the snails bury themselves, so sand and soil substrates are best. In nature they are usually found on sandy substrate; replicating this avoids constant stress that can shorten their life.

Aeration and flow: they appear to need high oxygen levels, as they are morphologically suited to life in streams with a surface current of 0–30 cm/sec.

Décor: not essential, but they appreciate leaves, rocks, wood, PVC pipes and so on. These give hiding places and surface area for algae and biofilm.

Chopstick snails are omnivorous scavengers and will consume any organic food available. In an aquarium they act as a clean-up crew against algae, biofilm, debris and waste.

Because of their size, supplementing their diet with vegetables and commercial foods is recommended. They will eat what you feed your fish and shrimp, for example shrimp pellets, shrimp granules, fish flakes and algae wafers. These sink to the bottom and stay there until the snails find them.

Calcium is needed for several vital processes in snails, most obviously shell formation.

Feeding frequency: 1–2 times a week.

Chopstick snails are non-aggressive and docile. They have no means of attacking other tank inhabitants and only their operculum and shell for protection. They can close the shell completely with the operculum when disturbed.

They are nocturnal: at night they crawl on the surface and may bury themselves or hide by day. This is common among grazing invertebrates and is mainly linked to avoiding visual predators while feeding. On a 24-hour cycle, dusk is when algae holds maximum nutrients, at the end of the photosynthetic period.

They are burrowers and continuously turn over the substrate, which helps prevent anaerobic pockets.

Generally they do not eat healthy plants, so they suit planted tanks, but they may dig up plants with weak root systems.

Features: social, active, peaceful, burrowers.

This species is not hermaphroditic. Stenomelania torulosa is gonochoristic (each individual is either male or female). No study describing how to distinguish males and females by external features has been found.

The reproductive biology of Chopstick snails is largely unknown. The pet industry depends entirely on wild-caught animals, and no successful captive breeding is known.

  • They develop from veliger larvae.
  • They are ovoviparous and carry eggs in a brood pouch until they hatch into a larval form.
  • In nature, females release free-swimming veligers from the brood pouch into freshwater, where water flow sweeps the larvae into brackish lagoons or the open sea.
  • The larvae cannot develop in freshwater. They live only under brackish-water influence, where they complete metamorphosis into small copies of adults.
  • The veligers feed on microplankton (phyto- and zooplankton).

It is not known how long development takes.

Description

The Chopstick snail is a relatively large snail, growing up to about 10 cm, though the average shell length is around 5–7 cm. The shell is elongated and sculptured with strong spiral ridges. The whorls are rather flat with no deep sutures; full-grown shells have 12–14 whorls. Colour ranges from light olive to dark brown. The shell is thick and strong, but the apex is often eroded. In young snails the top whorls are lighter and often spotted with small brown spots and lines; adults are mostly coated by a thick black layer. The cephalic tentacles are moderately long.

Lifespan

No data are available on lifespan in the wild. They can live 3–4 years in captivity if appropriately cared for.

Tankmates

They are harmless and a good choice for any peaceful community tank.

  • Fish: do not keep with big or aggressive fish such as Botia lohacata, cichlids, loaches and goldfish. Best tankmates are calm, peaceful fish such as Panda Garra, Pygmy Cory Catfish and Otocinclus Catfish.
  • Shrimp: species that prefer slightly alkaline water, such as vampire, bamboo, Amano, ghost, cherry, blue tiger, snowball, Caridina cf. babaulti, blue velvet, Malawa and ninja shrimp.
  • Snails: black devil snails, Brotia pagodula, rabbit snails, nerite snails, mystery snails, ramshorn snails, Malaysian trumpet snails and others. Do not keep with assassin snails.
  • Crayfish: not recommended with large crayfish and most freshwater crabs. Dwarf crayfish (Cambarellus diminutus, etc.) are too small to overpower the snail but may nip off its antennae periodically.

Pros and cons

Pros: large and gorgeous; fully freshwater snail that can tolerate brackish water; do not overpopulate the tank; good algae eaters and cleaners; peaceful; do not eat plants; burrow and aerate the substrate. Cons: produce a lot of waste; require good water flow; need brackish water to reproduce; can climb out of tanks.
